steps.label: Neuston
lines: Neustons are the animals that live at the
air-water interface, that is at the surface
Ex: water striders, beetles and water bugs
Ex: mosquito larvae stay just below the
steps.why: Neuston is fixed to one place, the surface film, and it has two named halves — above and below the film — so both are given, since either may be asked for by name.
common_mistakes: Writing that neustons swim in the water. They live AT the surface.
Mixing up the two halves. Epi is above the surface, hypo is below it.
steps.memory_tip: Epi is on top, hypo is under: the water strider walks on the film, the mosquito larva hangs below it.
steps.margin_note: One line for the place, then one example each for above and below.

steps.label: Nekton

lines.text: Neuston at the surface, nekton swimming

lines: Nektons are the animals that can swim
They move against the current under their
Ex: fishes, amphibians and water snakes.
steps.why: The distinction is where the animal lives and whether it can swim, so the second half states both — free swimming and moving against the current — which also separates nekton from plankton, which only drift.
common_mistakes: Calling plankton nekton. Plankton drift with the water; nekton swim against it.
Giving mosquito larvae as nekton. They belong to the neuston, below the surface film.
steps.memory_tip: Neuston lives on the line between air and water; nekton lives in the water and swims.
steps.margin_note: One line for swimming, one for the current, then the examples.

insider_note: The contrast is surface against open water — a student who writes swims for both terms loses one mark.
